# Commission: What a citation can support

## Intended contribution

Help a writer decide whether the material they retained supports the citation they want to make. Make the limit one of evidence, not a claim that writers cannot make unsupported assertions.

## Must keep

A paraphrase can preserve an idea without preserving the author's words. Quotation marks cannot recover those words. To claim greater precision or broader support, consult evidence that supplies what is missing. A successful wording check verifies a match under its comparison rule against the text actually used; it does not certify the original author, context, or truth. Missing evidence is not a pass.

## Must exclude

Do not teach the validator, survey checking techniques, or explain the two-layer storage design or its copyright history. Do not argue from legal or empirical claims.

## Reserved decisions

Keep the existing title and path. Do not split the note or edit its dependents. Publication requires operator approval.

## Current direction

Keep it short. Lead with the paraphrase versus direct quotation example. Use Commonplace's quote checker only to illustrate the principle, preferably in one sentence. Stop when the reader knows when to narrow the citation and when to return to the source.

# Note

Use `note` for transferable KB claims, observations, and theory that are worth preserving beyond the current task. A note is a structured markdown artifact with YAML frontmatter, a prose title, and enough body context for an agent to decide how to use it.

## Frontmatter

| Field | Required | Use |
|---|---:|---|
| `type` | Yes | `types/note.md` |
| `description` | Yes | Discriminating retrieval filter, not a summary. |
| `traits` | No | Independently checkable review expectations. |
| `tags` | No | Navigation tags used by indexes. |
| `user-verified` | No | May only be `true`; records explicit human attestation to the current substantive contents. |

## Description

The description should answer "why this document?" for a future retrieval decision. It should distinguish the note from nearby notes and usually fit in one sentence.

## User verification

`user-verified: true` means a human user explicitly attests that the artifact's current substantive contents have been verified. Absence means only that there is no current user attestation; it says nothing about truth, maturity, currency, or review history.

Creation, conversion, deterministic validation, and semantic review do not confer human verification; their outputs must not carry a newly granted `user-verified` field. After a substantive edit, the field must be absent until a human explicitly verifies the revised contents. An existing attestation remains valid across a mechanical change only when that change is covered by an explicit human-approved trivial-change workflow.

## Traits

Traits route semantic review. They do not change structural validation.

| Trait | What it asserts |
|---|---|
| `title-as-claim` | The title is a proposition that can be true or false. |
| `definition` | The note pins a term's operational meaning. |
| `has-comparison` | The note compares alternatives. |
| `has-external-sources` | The note cites material outside the project. |
| `has-implementation` | The note includes implementation sketches or code-facing detail. |
| `synthesis` | The note composes multiple cited claims into a unified argument; cite as a unit and expect inline restatement. Waives the default body-composability rule. |

## Writing Shape

- Use the title as the strongest compressed handle for the note.
- Put the main claim or mechanism near the top.
- Link to adjacent notes where the relationship helps traversal.
- Keep design rationale in notes; keep imperative procedure in instructions.
- State the claim's limits under their own heading (`## Scope`): assumptions, applicability conditions, known failure cases. A limit with its own section can be narrowed by a rescoping edit without rewriting the claim, and the review gates that test scope look for it. Omit the section when no limit is known. `structured-claim` notes use `## Caveats` for the same role.

## Template

```markdown
---
description: ""
type: types/note.md
traits: []
tags: []
---

# {prose-as-title — a proposition, not a topic label}

{Your analysis, reasoning, or exploration. Freeform.}

## Scope

- {Assumptions, applicability conditions, known failure cases — omit section if none}

## Open Questions

- {Unresolved points worth tracking — omit section if none}

---

Relevant Notes:

- [related-note](./related-note.md) — how it relates
```

---

Relevant Notes:

- [text](./text.md) - implicit no-frontmatter capture state that can be promoted to a note
- [document-types-should-be-verifiable](../theory/document-types-should-be-verifiable.md) - design rationale for verifiable types

# Writing conventions for kb/theory/

## Text contract and explanatory-reach

This collection retains **beliefs about the design space** — truth-apt claims
that explain how systems of this kind can work, including bounded claims about
one fixed design. A claim may be grounded in or bounded to a particular system,
including Commonplace, when it preserves the particular's proposition-relative
scope and contributes more than the selected value or resulting state.
Truth-aptness of a local observation alone does not place it here.

Apply the placement test to the artifact's intended contribution: **after every
named system choice is recoverably scoped, does a substantive claim about the
design space remain?** A fixed choice needs stable reidentification at every
distinction that could change truth or licensed inference. A ranged choice
needs a recoverable range and valuation rule. A substantive witness needs the
universal prohibition it contradicts or the existence claim it verifies. If scoping leaves only what Commonplace
selected or the current or historical state that selection produced, the
artifact belongs in `kb/reference/`.

The claim that remains after scoping is a new universal hypothesis, not a
summary of the particulars it came from: no number of singular observations
establishes a universal statement ([Popper, *Logic of Scientific Discovery*,
§§13–15](../sources/popper-logic-of-scientific-discovery.ingest.md)). Link the
cases it was generalized from as `abstracted-from`; they explain its origin
and do not corroborate it. A particular system may still appear as the case a
universal claim is applied to: the claim supplies the law, and the system's
selections supply the initial conditions (§12).

Quality goal is **explanatory-reach** — the most general formulation the argument supports, with boundaries mapped. A note with explanatory-reach compresses many situations into one explanation.

Tests for explanatory-reach:
- Change one premise — can you predict the change in the conclusion?
- Would the insight apply in a different domain?
- Could someone say exactly how it's wrong, not just that it's incomplete?
- Does it account for where the pattern actually works and fails, not just why it should?

Notes that only record "X works" are adaptive — useful but brittle. Explaining *why* X works gives explanatory-reach. Explanatory-reach is a direction, not a gate.

Apply explanatory-reach to claim formulation:
- State the claim under the weakest assumptions the argument actually uses.
- Treat qualifiers in the title, description, opening claim, and main proof as obligations. If a qualifier does not change the reasoning when removed, drop it from the claim or move it to an application, corollary, or scope note.
- Keep real boundaries explicit. A boundary belongs in the claim when the argument depends on it; otherwise it belongs in `## Scope`, `## Caveats`, or a nearby narrower application note.
- Prefer a general lemma plus narrower consequences over a narrow lemma whose extra assumptions are only needed by one downstream use.

**Don't defend against objections you've already closed.** A clause that pre-empts a misreading the previous clause already ruled out doesn't add rigor, it pads: "a hypothesis to be tested, not a definitional truth" — being a hypothesis to be tested already means it isn't one. State the claim once; let review catch what still needs defending.

**Admit real gaps instead of hedging around them.** Precision means an agent can't misread the claim — it does not mean stacking qualifications against every conceivable pushback. When the argument has an actual gap — an assumption you can't yet defend, a case you haven't worked through — name it plainly in `## Scope` or `## Open Questions` as an opening for later investigation. A named gap is more useful than one padded shut with defensive language, and it's what review and later notes are for.

**Formulation constraint — scope the choices you name.** For every named system
choice, the title, description, and opening argument must preserve the
proposition-relative reference rule or range and the role that choice plays.
Those can come from the surface itself or from context the intended consumer is
guaranteed to receive. A fixed opaque design may use stable reidentification
when hidden identity distinctions cannot change truth or licensed inference. A
ranged variable needs a recoverable range and valuation rule. A substantive
witness must state which universal prohibition the instance contradicts or
which existence claim it verifies; a single instance cannot support a
universal claim (§15). Literal quantifier
syntax is neither necessary nor sufficient. Substitution can expose dependence
on a local term, but the consumption boundary decides whether its scope is
missing. If no substantive claim remains after each choice is scoped, move the
artifact to `kb/reference/` because its intended contribution is what
Commonplace selected or the state that selection produced. Claims later in the
body obey the same scoping rule; explicitly scoped local reports and examples
may serve as the theory's origin, illustration, or test without becoming the
artifact's intended contribution; only a test counts as corroboration (see
"Origin is not corroboration").

**Theory-independence constraint.** The claim must stand if any single cited description is removed — otherwise it's still a description.

**Design-shaped artifacts need a theoretical claim.** A construction may stay here when it witnesses a substantive truth-apt existential claim. Mark its [residual selections as choices](./artifact-classification-separates-content-kind-lineage-and-authority.md), not as evidence that the selections are uniquely correct. The requirements must be substantive enough that exhibiting any witness is informative; otherwise the unadopted design belongs in `kb/reference/proposals/` under [ADR 028](../reference/adr/028-design-proposals-live-in-reference-proposals.md). Proposal status is a workflow state, not an information kind.

**Hypotheses stay recognizable in prose.** State the conjectural force in the title, description, opening, or a clearly named hypotheses/open-questions section. `user-verified: true` may attest that a note responsibly presents a conjecture; it does not turn the conjecture into established fact.

**Claim modality (ADR 066, ADR 091).** A claim asserts in one of three modes, and the mode determines what refutes it. **Universal** — the default reading for any claim that does not state otherwise. A counterexample refutes it when others can check it again: a specified case whose conflict with the claim any reader can re-derive, or an observed effect shown to recur. A single unrepeated report of an exception raises a problem to test; it does not by itself refute ([Popper, *Logic of Scientific Discovery*, §22](../sources/popper-logic-of-scientific-discovery.ingest.md)). A contradiction refutes the claim together with the conditions it was applied under (§18), so a refutation names which part it blames: the claim, or those conditions. **Statistical** — the claim states a tendency ("usually", "most", "under conditions C"); a single instance does not refute it, prevalence evidence does — and the claim must still forbid something: state the comparison, conditions, or rate that prevalence evidence could refute, or the tendency is vacuous. This stated-refuter requirement is Popper's treatment of probabilistic claims (§§65–68) made per-claim: a frequency claim is strictly unfalsifiable until a refuting prevalence is fixed in advance, and here that decision lives in the claim text rather than in a field-wide convention. **Ideal-type** — the claim states a deliberately simple first-order model whose exceptions are conceded and accounted for; what refutes it is an exception the domain treats as ordinary unmarked practice, or the model losing explanatory dominance — see [domain pricing routes an exception to idealization assessment but does not decide it](./domain-pricing-routes-an-exception-to-idealization-assessment.md). Ideal-type acceptance and refutation are comparative — inference to the best explanation with its virtues (declared use, mechanism, bound, dominance) written as attackable commitments rather than reviewer judgment; the bound is absolute, so "best available" alone never suffices. A priced exception is Lakatos's anomaly rather than a refuter: it earns the claim an idealization assessment, and the adequacy record then decides the verdict. Declare the mode in the claim text itself — title, thesis, or a named section; an ideal-type claim carries its adequacy record (declared use, omitted mechanism, consequence bound, explanatory dominance) in the body, where review attacks it like any content. There is no frontmatter mode field: undeclared text reads as universal. Mode is orthogonal to lifecycle stage — a note still at the conjecture stage may conjecture a universal or a tendency; declare both when both apply. Repair under review is mode-aware and runs in both directions: reframing a defeated universal down to statistical or ideal-type requires meeting the target mode's guard, and a claim hedged below its warrant is reframed up, not left vacuous.

## Title and body composability

**Claim titles by default.** Name the note like a claim, not a topic — something that could be true or false.

- *Composability test:* `since [title](./title.md)` or `because [title](./title.md)` reads naturally as prose.
- *Strength test:* the claim is contestable. "Continuous learning can happen outside of weights" passes; "continuous learning is substrate-independent" fails — nobody pushes back.

Add the `title-as-claim` trait when using one, so review gates check the promise.

**Body composability.** Another note should be able to cite this one as a premise without inheriting unrelated claims or examples. If a second cluster would poison imports, split it off or move it to `kb/work/`.

Exception: notes with the `synthesis` trait weave multiple cited claims into a single argument and are cited as a unit. Component claims that need to stand as citable premises should be extracted into their own notes.

Exceptions to claim titles: multi-claim specs, definitions, indexes, and exploratory drafts not ready to assert.

## Outbound links

Author each outbound link from the reader need at its source. A reciprocal link is allowed when the reverse direction independently helps readers; never add one merely to mirror an existing edge. Relationship symmetry describes semantics, not an authoring obligation: `contradicts` and `contrasts` are self-dual, while the other labels are directional. Find inbound links on demand with repository search; no backlink view is currently generated. Inline for strongest commitment, with a connective word that fits the argument (e.g. `since [title](path)`, `because [title](path)`, `but [title](path)`, `as in [title](path)`). Footer for labelled — `- [title](path) — label: context phrase`.

Scan `kb/theory/`, `kb/types/`, `kb/reference/`, `kb/agent-memory-systems/`, `kb/agentic-systems/`, `kb/sources/`, `kb/instructions/`, and `kb/tags/` for link targets. Do not link into `kb/work/` (workshop layer — value is consumed, not imported). Most links land within `kb/theory/` — the densest path. Outbound edges to `kb/instructions/` are rare — the usual direction is inverse (`instruction → note` via `rests-on`) — except `operationalized-from`, recorded as an `Operationalized into:` footer at this collection's methodology note when a procedure in `kb/instructions/` adds ordering, defaults, or stopping conditions the methodology doesn't itself fix; see the lineage semantics in `kb/reference/link-vocabulary.md`. Edges to `kb/sources/` point to the tracked ingest of the source the claim was abstracted from or that corroborates it, never to its local snapshot.

**Origin is not corroboration.** Evidence corroborates a claim only when it reports an attempt to refute that claim which the claim could have failed ([Popper, *Logic of Scientific Discovery*, §82 and appendix \*ix](../sources/popper-logic-of-scientific-discovery.ingest.md)). The rule is the same for internal evidence (session traces, reports, ADRs) and external sources; what decides is how the evidence was produced, not where it came from. A case or source the claim was built from is linked `abstracted-from`, never as corroboration of that claim. An `evidenced-by` link that claims corroboration says in its context phrase what the claim risked, and whether the evidence was recorded after the claim or independently of how it was built; otherwise the phrase says the evidence qualifies or bounds the claim. A corroboration appraisal is dated: it holds relative to the evidence accepted when it was made (§84).

**Labels:**

| label | kind | destinations | reader-need |
|---|---|---|---|
| `extends` | asym | theory | wants the argument developed further |
| `grounds` | asym | theory | wants to verify the premise |
| `enables` | asym | theory | wants the operational prerequisite |
| `exemplifies` | asym (instance→general) | theory | wants the general claim this instance falls under |
| `mechanism` | asym | theory | wants to understand how the claim operates |
| `contradicts` | sym | theory | wants to resolve a disagreement |
| `contrasts` | sym | theory | wants the neighbouring-shape distinction |
| `defined-in` | asym | theory/definitions, reference/definitions | reader may not know the term |
| `evidenced-by` | asym | theory, types, reference, reports/retained, agent-memory-systems, agentic-systems, sources, external | the target observation, case, or source corroborates, qualifies, or bounds this assertion; corroboration requires a test the claim could have failed (see "Origin is not corroboration") |
| `derived-from` | asym | reference, agent-memory-systems, agentic-systems, sources | claim is worked out from this source, adding nothing beyond it — see the lineage semantics in `kb/reference/link-vocabulary.md` |
| `abstracted-from` | asym | theory/evidence, reference, reports/retained, agent-memory-systems, agentic-systems, sources | claim generalizes beyond this source; the source is evidence, authority is earned by testing |
| `operationalized-from` | asym | instructions | procedure adds ordering, defaults, or stopping conditions this methodology note doesn't itself fix; not claim-preserving — see lineage semantics in `kb/reference/link-vocabulary.md` |
| `see-also` | asym | reference, agent-memory-systems, agentic-systems, sources, instructions | adjacent companion; use sparingly |

## Source grounding

A note's grounding check must fit one pass, so the note is bounded on the artifact side ([ADR 082](../reference/adr/082-grounding-is-bounded-on-the-artifact-by-unquoted-sources.md)): at most five distinct tracked sources (`kb/sources/*.ingest.md`) cited without a verbatim quotation paired to each. This contract sets the bound in its `unquoted-source-limit` field, so it holds for every artifact here, definitions and proposals included ([ADR 122](../reference/adr/122-collections-set-the-unquoted-source-limit.md)); `commonplace-validate` fails past five. A source is discharged by quoting it: a quoted span in the same paragraph as its link, marked `verbatim`, whose words occur in that ingest's `## Quotes` section — retain the quote through `cp-skill-ground`, never by editing the ingest. A source linked with `(snapshot required)` anywhere in the note always counts. Links to other notes never count; a linked note has passed its own grounding review, and this note owes it faithful representation, not re-grounding. Over the bound, quote or split by claim; a claim carried jointly by several sources is quoted together, not split.

Two conventions keep the bound honest:

- **A source cited as evidence is cited in the body.** A footer-only source citation has no sentence to carry its use, so nothing in the note can be checked against it and nothing can quote it. Either host it in a sentence or drop the entry.
- **A casebook hosts its retained evidence in prose.** When sources sit in table rows, put the quotes in a short block under the table — one sentence per source, naming the row — rather than in the cells.

## Definition placement

Definitions whose intended contribution supplies vocabulary for transferable
theory belong under `kb/theory/definitions/`. Definitions constituted by a
Commonplace selection, contract, or implemented classification belong under
`kb/reference/definitions/`. The `definition` type does not decide placement.

## Evidence placement

Use `kb/theory/evidence/` when a note's primary contribution is what a bounded dataset, experiment, trace cohort, or comparative casebook establishes about the design space. Apply the placement test to the inference: when, after Commonplace's choices are scoped, it concerns only those fixed choices or their measured effects (no free variable), the evidence note belongs in `kb/reports/retained/` beside the raw evidence, keeping the note type; a theory note may still cite it. These remain theoretical notes under this collection contract: state both the inference the evidence supports and its limit. The larger theory may still be incomplete, but the evidence artifact must make its own bounded inference. Keep observations whose theory-facing inference is unresolved in `kb/work/`; put first occurrences and pure pattern records without explanation in `kb/log.md`. Put raw captures in `kb/sources/` and descriptions retained to represent a particular system's current or historical state in that system's descriptive collection.

## Proposal placement

Use `kb/theory/proposals/` for finished theory the KB has not decided to import into its vocabulary: frameworks, distinctions, terms, and changes to adopted definitions. Placement follows adoption state, not doubt about the content; a conjecture that needs no new vocabulary is an ordinary note that states its conjectural force. Every artifact under `proposals/` carries the collection-local [`theory-proposal`](./types/theory-proposal.md) type, which states what a proposal must contain and how it is adopted or deleted ([ADR 084](../reference/adr/084-kind-rules-live-in-type-specs-and-operations-in-instructions.md)). Other notes may point to a proposal but do not cite it as a premise or use its terms as settled vocabulary.

## What does NOT belong here

- Unadopted system designs → `kb/reference/proposals/` (`design-proposal` type), unless recast as an existential claim per above
- Records of what Commonplace selected, and descriptions of the current or historical state those selections produced → `kb/reference/`
- Descriptions of a specific system's contract, interface, or current construction → `kb/reference/` for Commonplace, or `kb/agent-memory-systems/` and `kb/agentic-systems/` for external systems
- Procedures and how-to guidance → `kb/instructions/`
- Raw captures without frontmatter → `text` type, any collection
- Work in progress → `kb/work/` (workshops)

# A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

Marking a span as an exact quotation asserts that these words occur in a named source. Unchecked, that assertion rests on the author's word. A quote check makes it falsifiable by testing one relation: given a quoted span, a resolved source text and a normalization rule, does the span occur in that text, once or once inside a stated range? Markers that never claimed exact wording, such as a paraphrase marker, give the check nothing to match.

## Four questions, one answered mechanically

A citation raises four separable questions:

1. Wording: do these words occur in the compared text?
2. Attribution: is the compared text the source the citation names, and did the named author produce it?
3. Context: does the passage, read where it occurs, support the use the citing text makes of it?
4. Truth: is the quoted claim true?

A string check answers only the wording question. An identity check answers part of the second question (below). Context needs a reader of both texts. Wording agreement is deterministic, cheap and binary, so it can run on every pass. Judging support is costlier and noisier, so it cannot simply block the way a wording check does, and how reliably it detects out-of-context use is unmeasured.

For an exact-wording claim, an inexpensive occurrence check can justify treating mismatch as failure rather than warning. This is a choice within the [trade-off between checking cost and reliance risk](./checking-retained-results-trades-cost-against-reliance-risk.md), not a universal rule for retained results. Later readers can reuse the check's result, accepting the risk of changes since it ran.

## What makes "exact" meaningful

"Exact" means "equal after this normalization rule", and the rule can err in both directions. Too little normalization fails correct quotes on quote marks or whitespace; [ADR 046](../reference/adr/046-verbatim-quotes-are-validated-against-their-cited-source.md) judges such false mismatches worse than no check. Too much would let substantive edits pass. In one casebook corpus the real mismatches were mostly editorial omissions, bracketed substitutions and case changes (ADR 046), which a permissive enough rule would ignore. Typography and emphasis can affect meaning in prose as well as code; a normalization rule must specify which differences it ignores.

Occurrence is not location. A span can occur several times, and a plausible line range can point elsewhere in the same file. Requiring exactly one occurrence, or exactly one complete occurrence inside a checked range, removes ambiguity about which passage the span equals. Forbidding concatenation of disjoint ranges prevents certifying a passage that never existed contiguously (ADR 094). Uniqueness does not establish that the author intended this occurrence. A locator the check does not test supplies context but is not evidence.

## Which evidence a pass is relative to

A pass means "agrees with the evidence this check used". That evidence may be the original, a capture (a retained copy of the source bytes taken at one time), an intermediary's retained extract, or nothing.

Source identity comes first. A checksum against a recorded capture, with explicit name pairing between citation and file, binds the compared bytes to that capture; equal bytes at an arbitrary path do not (ADR 073). A mismatched or unreadable file is a failure, not an invitation to find another copy. The binding stops at the capture: no mechanism here checks that the capture faithfully represents the original or that the named author wrote it. A pin records identity, and change is detected only when a later check compares current bytes with it. Checking current bytes catches a changed or removed passage at the next check, but misses a changed surrounding context when the quoted words survive.

Retained, accessible and used material differ. A capture kept on another machine is not evidence for a check on this one, and neither is text that happens to sit in a model's context. Missing bytes therefore report as unverified, never as passed. A silent fallback to whatever copy is present would make one citation pass or fail with ambient cache state, without declaring that dependency (ADR 073).

A model may need several reads to check a source that exceeds its context budget. Each excerpt can preserve the wording exactly while omitting context needed to judge the quotation’s use. The checker must retrieve that context before judging support; the full source can remain stored outside the model’s context.

Exactness and second-hand provenance are independent. A quote can be exact with respect to an intermediary's extract and second-hand with respect to the original. Each exact check in a chain, such as capture to extract and extract to note, verifies only its own pair. Semantic hops compound instead: checking a paraphrase against a paraphrase adds a judgment at each hop, and rewording at either hop can change the proposition. Checking against verified source extracts avoids judging a paraphrase of a paraphrase.

## Scope

- Covers textual sources with retrievable bytes. Audio, images, oral quotation and sources whose original is gone are out of scope.
- Transfer beyond agent-operated KBs rests on the reasoning above, not on external evidence.
- Marked editorial alterations (ellipsis, brackets) fail a strict wording assertion; whether a segment-wise check could support them is open.
- An "unresolved" outcome covers recognized quote candidates the checker could not pair with a source. Quotations the extractor never recognized appear in no outcome, and their rate is unmeasured.

# Reconstruction: what a citation can support

Basis for the commissioned contribution: help a writer decide whether the material they retained supports the citation they want to make, framed as a limit of evidence. No write brief was supplied; the commission alone states intent, must-keep, must-exclude and reserved decisions. The commission and the source list agree.

Source paths:

- S1 = `kb/reference/adr/073-untracked-source-snapshots-require-ingest-grounding.md` (input `source-1`). Role: what a retained passage can support versus what requires returning to the source.
- S2 = `kb/reference/adr/046-verbatim-quotes-are-validated-against-their-cited-source.md` (input `source-2`). Role: what the Commonplace wording check tests, for one illustration only.

## Support

### C1. An interpretation or paraphrase is not source text

- S1, Context ¶1: an ingest's "summaries, classifications, connection judgments, and limitations are interpretations. They are not source text." Tracking them does not change this (S1, Consequences ¶1: ingest analysis "cannot acquire source authority by being tracked").
- S1, Context ¶2: checking a claim against a paraphrase that was itself checked against the source "creates two semantic hops, and rewording at either hop can change the proposition". A paraphrase ledger "makes the judgment easier to run but not sound."
- S1, Considered alternatives, "Keep the paraphrased Claims ledger": review then "depend[s] on a paraphrase of a paraphrase. The semantic relation that matters remains indirect."
- S2, Consequences ¶1: the `paraphrase layer` and `second-hand` markers "never claimed exact text, and no derivation rule exists for them". (This sentence then links the note being rewritten as its rationale; see Conflicts.)

Neither source states in so many words that a paraphrase preserves the idea while losing the words. S1 supports the weaker and related point that rewording can change the proposition, and that an interpretation is not source text.

### C2. A verbatim citation asserts exact copying from a retained source

- S2, Context ¶1: "A `verbatim` citation asserts that a quoted span is copied exactly from a source retained in the KB."
- S2, Decision, mismatch bullet: a mismatch means "The note asserts false textual fidelity", and "a reader who trusts that assertion may skip source comparison and miss the error."
- S2, Context ¶3: real mismatches were "dominated by editorial omission (`...`), bracketed substitution, case changes, and punctuation moved inside the quotation boundary". These are concrete ways quotation marks are put around words that are not the source's words. (The surrounding counts are empirical; the commission excludes arguing from them.)

### C3. A bounded retained passage can support some uses; others require the full source

- S1, Context ¶3: "A bounded verbatim passage may contain enough source material to judge the note's use. Some claims instead depend on broad, distributed, or contextual material that cannot be represented soundly by a small set of retained quotes. The full snapshot is then required, but it cannot be assumed to exist on every machine."
- S1, Decision, quotes route: when the retained quotes are used as support, "If the quotes are insufficient, the check fails; it never silently falls back to a local snapshot."
- S1, Decision ¶ after routes: writers "apply the same gate to that inference rather than asking the source to contain the target's conclusion" — transfer reasoning belongs to the citing text, not the source.
- S1, Decision ¶2: the retained material is "the minimum one or more exact passages needed for a sound later check".

### C4. Missing evidence is a failure, not a pass

- S1, Decision, snapshot route: "Missing, mismatched, or unreadable bytes are a failure, not a warning or an invitation to find another copy."
- S1, Considered alternatives, "Let the checker fall back to any available snapshot automatically": this "would make the same note pass or fail according to ambient cache state without declaring that dependency."
- S1, Consequences ¶1: a fresh checkout "must fail declared snapshot-dependent uses until the exact observation is restored."
- S2, Consequences ¶3: "The extraction heuristic is not complete, and `unresolved` is how it says so rather than passing silently."
- S2, Decision, unresolved bullet: `unresolved` warns, and only in notes carrying at least one resolvable verbatim quote. Unresolved is never counted as a match.

### C5. What a successful wording check verifies, and what it does not

- S2, Context ¶2: "the comparison rule is a substring test under the checker’s normalization; the adjacent Markdown link locates the source; and the checked-in source is available at validation time. Location alone does not establish availability." Checker trustworthiness "needs separate support".
- S2, Consequences ¶3: normalization is "quote-mark folding, whitespace collapse, emphasis stripping, `NFKC`". A match is therefore a match under that rule, not byte equality.
- S2, Decision ¶1: the check resolves the quotation "against the markdown source it links" — i.e. against the text actually linked and used.
- S1, Considered alternatives, "Store a verbatim copy of every note claim": "string equality would still not establish source support."
- S1, Consequences ¶2: "source locations remain authored locators rather than mechanically verified anchors" — the location (and so the surrounding context) is not checked.
- S1, Considered alternatives, "Use checksum-first lookup": "Equal bytes do not bind a local path to the ingest being cited."
- S2, Consequences ¶1: `verbatim` is "the only one [marker] that can be mechanically falsified".

## Inference

- I1 (quotation marks cannot recover words). From C1 (interpretations are not source text; rewording can change the proposition) and C2 (a verbatim citation asserts exact copying from a retained source): if only a paraphrase was retained, there is no retained text from which exact words could be copied, so a verbatim citation built on it asserts something the retained material cannot back. The sources do not state this directly; it combines C1 and C2.
- I2 (narrow the citation or return to the source). From C3: when the retained passage is enough to judge the use, the citation can stand on it; when the use depends on broad, distributed or contextual material, the retained passage is insufficient and the full source is needed. Combined with C4, a writer without the full source has two honest options: narrow the claim (or its fidelity marker, e.g. to paraphrase) to what the retained material supports, or obtain the source. Silently relying on unavailable material is not an option. The "narrow" option is an inference: S1 describes failure on insufficiency and the snapshot requirement, not rescoping as a remedy; S2's paraphrase/second-hand markers (C1) show weaker-fidelity citations exist.
- I3 (a pass certifies a match, not the source). From C5: the check compares the quoted span against the linked text under a normalization rule. It therefore cannot establish that the linked text is the original author's words, that the span keeps its context (locators are unverified), or that the quoted claim is true (string equality does not establish source support). "Original author" and "truth" are not named in either source; this extends S1's "string equality would still not establish source support" and S2's statement that the check runs against the linked source.
- I4 (the limit is evidential, not a ban on assertion). From C2 and C4: the check fails a citation for asserting fidelity its evidence lacks; S1 frames the gate as matching each claim to the input that can support it. Neither source frames this as forbidding unsupported claims in general; a writer may still make a claim at the fidelity its retained material supports.
- I5 (general principle beyond Commonplace). Both sources describe Commonplace choices. The general claim — a citation's asserted fidelity is bounded by what its retained capture preserves — is a generalization from these cases (`abstracted-from`), not something they corroborate.

## Conflicts

- S2 internal tension: Context ¶1 says a verbatim citation asserts the span "is copied exactly", while Context ¶2 and Consequences ¶3 define the check as a substring test under normalization (quote folding, whitespace collapse, emphasis stripping, NFKC). So a pass is weaker than "exactly". This supports the commission's "a match under its comparison rule"; a writer should not equate a pass with exact identity.
- S2 cites the note being rewritten: S2 Consequences ¶1 explains the unchecked markers with "which is precisely why [a citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved](...)". This is a dependence of S2 on the note, not independent support for it; using it as support would be circular.
- Availability: S2 Context ¶2 assumes "the checked-in source is available at validation time"; S1 Context ¶1 and ¶3 say the full captured source is not retained in a fresh checkout and "cannot be assumed to exist on every machine". These concern different source kinds (tracked retained quotes versus untracked full captures) and do not contradict each other, but the availability condition the check relies on does not hold for every source.
- Currency of S1: S1 header says it is amended by ADR 076 (quote append moved to grounding) and ADR 094 (attributed blocks, unique occurrences, checked ranges); "The text below records the earlier decision." Neither amendment is an authorized source. The distinctions used here (C3, C4) are not marked as superseded, but mechanism details in S1 may be stale.

## Scope

- Both sources describe Commonplace decisions (ADRs). Their support is for Commonplace's citation markers, routes and validator; the general claim is an abstraction from them (I5).
- S2's check applies only to `verbatim`-marked quotations with an adjacent link to a Markdown source that is available at check time. It reports `unresolved` when extraction fails, and that warning appears only in notes with at least one resolvable verbatim quote (S2 Decision). Code-fenced examples are excluded from checking (S2 Decision ¶ on code).
- S2: the checker's own trustworthiness "needs separate support"; the prototype audit gives bounded evidence only, and no check-cost measurement is recorded (S2 Context ¶2).
- S1's bounded-versus-full distinction is stated for source-dependent claims checked against ingest quotes or a pinned snapshot. "Broad, distributed, or contextual" is the stated class needing the full source; S1 gives no finer test for deciding which class a claim falls into.
- Commission exclusions bound use of the sources: do not teach the validator, survey checking techniques, explain the tracked/untracked (two-layer) storage design or copyright history, or argue from legal or empirical claims (so the prototype counts in S2 and the corpus counts in S1 are not to be used as argument). Use S2 for one illustrative sentence only.

## Gaps

- No source defines "fidelity" or "capture" as used in the title. "Capture" is closest to S1's "complete captured source" / "exact captured bytes"; "fidelity" appears only in S2's "false textual fidelity".
- No source states that a paraphrase preserves the idea while losing the words; S1 supports only that rewording can change the proposition (C1). The must-keep's positive half (a paraphrase *can* preserve an idea) is unsupported and would rest on the author's own argument.
- No source states that "quotation marks cannot recover those words"; this is inference I1.
- No source explicitly says a wording check does not certify the original author, the context, or truth. Support is partial (C5, I3): string equality does not establish source support; locators are not verified; the check runs against the linked text.
- No source names "narrowing the citation" as the remedy when retained material is insufficient; S1 names only failure and the full-source requirement (I2).
- No source supplies a decision rule for when a retained passage is "enough" beyond S1's bounded-versus-broad/distributed/contextual contrast. The commission's stopping point ("when to narrow the citation and when to return to the source") relies on that contrast plus inference.
- Neither source supplies a paraphrase-versus-direct-quotation example of the kind the commission asks to lead with; the author must construct it. S2's mismatch kinds (omission with `...`, bracketed substitution, case changes, moved punctuation) are available as raw material.

claim-account.text:
# Claim account: a citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

No write brief was supplied. The commission alone carries intent, must-keep,
must-exclude, reserved decisions and current direction. It does not conflict
with the reconstruction's source list. No problem file is needed.

Overall shape the commitments below assume: a short `kb/theory/` note with a
claim title (title and path are reserved; keep them). It opens with a
constructed paraphrase-versus-direct-quotation example, states the general
principle, gives the two exits (narrow the citation, or return to the source),
says what a passed wording check does and does not show, uses Commonplace's
quote checker in at most one illustrative sentence, and ends with `## Scope`.
It stops once the reader knows when to narrow and when to return to the
source. The claim is universal: a citation's asserted fidelity is bounded by
what the retained capture preserves. Its origin is the two ADRs, linked as
`abstracted-from`, not as corroboration.

## 1. Lead example: paraphrase versus direct quotation

- **Commitment.** A writer who retained only a paraphrase of a passage cannot
  present that passage as a direct quotation. A writer who retained the exact
  passage can.
- **Treatment.** State it, as a constructed example. The commission requires
  the note to lead with it.
- **Basis.** No source supplies such an example (Gaps). The author constructs
  it. S2's mismatch kinds are allowed as raw material for how quotation marks
  end up around words that are not the source's words (C2): editorial
  omission with `...`, bracketed substitution, case changes, and punctuation
  moved inside the quotation boundary. The prototype counts must not be used.
- **Scope and qualifiers.** Keep it generic: a writer, a source, a retained
  note or excerpt. Do not tie it to Commonplace's ingest or snapshot
  machinery.
- **Dependencies.** It sets up commitments 2 and 3.
- **Destination.** The opening paragraph or paragraphs, before the general
  statement.

## 2. A paraphrase can preserve an idea without preserving the author's words

- **Commitment.** Paraphrase and quotation preserve different things.
  Rewording can keep the idea, but it drops the wording. Rewording can also
  change the proposition.
- **Treatment.** State it with a qualifier. The commission requires the
  positive half ("can preserve an idea"). The sources do not state it. It
  rests on the author's own argument: rewording is what makes something a
  paraphrase. Present it as the note's own reasoning, not as a sourced
  finding. Add the sourced cautionary half: rewording can change the
  proposition, and an interpretation is not source text.
- **Basis.** C1. S1, Context ¶1: interpretations "are not source text".
  S1, Context ¶2: rewording at either hop "can change the proposition". The
  positive half has no source support (Gaps).
- **Scope and qualifiers.** "Can". Do not claim a paraphrase reliably
  preserves the idea. Do not cite S2's paraphrase or second-hand markers as
  support for this note, because that S2 passage cites this note (Conflicts).
- **Dependencies.** None. Commitments 3 and 5 depend on it.
- **Destination.** Directly after the example, as the principle the example
  shows.

## 3. Quotation marks cannot recover words the capture did not keep

- **Commitment.** A direct quotation asserts that the quoted words are the
  source's words. If the retained material holds only a paraphrase, it has
  no words that could back that assertion. Adding quotation marks to the
  paraphrase claims fidelity the capture did not preserve. This is the
  note's central claim and the title's proposition.
- **Treatment.** State it as inference. It is the note's own argument and is
  the general claim abstracted from the cases (I1, I5).
- **Basis.** I1, which combines C1 with C2. S2, Context ¶1: a verbatim
  citation "asserts that a quoted span is copied exactly from a source
  retained". S2, Decision: a mismatch means the note "asserts false textual
  fidelity". A reader who trusts the assertion may skip source comparison and
  miss the error. This reader consequence may be used as the reason the limit
  matters.
- **Scope and qualifiers.** General, not Commonplace-specific. "Fidelity"
  and "capture" are not defined in either source (Gaps). The note should make
  them plain in context. "Capture" means what was retained. "Fidelity" means
  how closely the citation claims to reproduce the source: exact words,
  idea, or location and context. Do not build a definition around them.
- **Dependencies.** Commitments 1 and 2.
- **Destination.** Opening claim, immediately after commitment 2. It may be
  generalized in one sentence beyond wording to any fidelity claim (greater
  precision, broader support), which leads into commitment 4.

## 4. A bounded retained passage supports some uses; others need the full source

- **Commitment.** A small exact retained passage can be enough to judge some
  uses of a source. Uses that depend on broad, distributed or contextual
  material cannot be soundly supported by a few retained passages and need
  the full source.
- **Treatment.** State it, framed generally. This is the criterion for the
  reader's decision.
- **Basis.** C3. S1, Context ¶3 gives the bounded-versus-broad, distributed
  or contextual contrast. S1, Decision ¶2: retain the minimum exact passages
  needed for a sound later check.
- **Scope and qualifiers.** S1 gives no finer test for deciding which class a
  claim falls into (Scope, Gaps). The note must not invent one. Name the
  absence in `## Scope` or `## Open Questions` if useful. The note may add
  that transfer reasoning belongs to the citing text: do not ask the source
  to contain the citer's conclusion (S1, Decision). It is optional; keep it
  only if it fits the brevity requirement.
- **Dependencies.** Commitment 3.
- **Destination.** Body, after the central claim. It sets up the exits.

## 5. Two honest exits: narrow the citation or return to the source

- **Commitment.** To claim greater precision or broader support than the
  retained material preserves, consult evidence that supplies what is
  missing. Otherwise, narrow the citation to what the capture supports, for
  example a paraphrase attribution instead of a quotation, or a narrower
  claim. Silently relying on material that is not available is not an
  option.
- **Treatment.** State the return-to-source half (must-keep, C3). State the
  narrow half as inference (I2). This commitment is where the note stops: the
  commission ends the note when the reader knows when to narrow and when to
  return.
- **Basis.** C3. S1: when the retained material is insufficient, "the full
  snapshot is then required". C4: failure, not silent fallback. I2:
  narrowing is not named by any source as a remedy (Gaps). It is the author's
  inference, informed by the existence of weaker-fidelity citation forms.
- **Scope and qualifiers.** Do not attribute "narrow the citation" to the
  sources. Do not cite S2's paraphrase or second-hand markers as independent
  support (circular; Conflicts). Use the decision rule from commitment 4 only
  at its stated grain.
- **Dependencies.** Commitments 3 and 4. It also depends on commitment 7
  (missing evidence is not a pass).
- **Destination.** The closing body section, before `## Scope`. End the
  argument here.

## 6. The limit is one of evidence, not a ban on assertion

- **Commitment.** The principle bounds what a citation may claim about its
  evidence. It does not forbid a writer from making a claim. A writer can
  still make the claim at the fidelity the retained material supports, or
  as their own assertion.
- **Treatment.** State it as inference (I4). The commission requires this
  framing ("Make the limit one of evidence").
- **Basis.** I4, from C2 and C4. S1 frames the gate as matching each claim to
  the input that can support it.
- **Scope and qualifiers.** One sentence is enough. The collection contract
  says not to defend against objections already closed, so do not repeat
  this framing.
- **Dependencies.** Commitment 3.
- **Destination.** Near the opening claim, as its framing. Alternatively,
  inside commitment 5's exits, where "narrow" shows that the claim survives
  at lower fidelity.

## 7. Missing evidence is not a pass

- **Commitment.** When the material needed to check a citation is absent,
  the citation is unsupported, not confirmed. Treating an absent source or an
  unresolved check as success makes the result depend on whatever happens to
  be at hand.
- **Treatment.** State it. It is a must-keep, and the sources support it
  directly.
- **Basis.** C4. S1: missing or unreadable bytes are "a failure, not a
  warning". Falling back to an ambient copy would make the same note pass or
  fail according to cache state. S2: `unresolved` is how the check reports
  incompleteness "rather than passing silently". It is never counted as a
  match.
- **Scope and qualifiers.** State it generally. Do not describe the snapshot
  route, ingest routes, or which notes the `unresolved` warning appears in.
  That would teach the validator (excluded).
- **Dependencies.** None. It supports commitment 5.
- **Destination.** One sentence in or beside commitment 5, or beside
  commitment 8.

## 8. A successful wording check verifies a match under its rule against the text used, nothing more

- **Commitment.** A passed wording check shows that the quoted span matches
  the text actually linked, under the check's comparison rule. It does not
  certify that the linked text is the original author's words, that the span
  keeps its original context, or that the quoted claim is true.
- **Treatment.** State the positive part directly (C5). State the "does not
  certify author, context or truth" part as inference (I3), worded as
  following from what the check compares. It is a must-keep.
- **Basis.** C5. S2: the comparison is a substring test under normalization,
  against the linked Markdown source. S1: "string equality would still not
  establish source support". Locators are authored, not mechanically
  verified. Equal bytes do not bind a path to the cited ingest. I3: neither
  source names "original author" or "truth" (Gaps).
- **Scope and qualifiers.** S2 internal tension (Conflicts): S2 says a
  verbatim citation asserts exact copying, but its check is a normalized
  substring test. A pass is a match under the rule, not exact identity. The
  note should say "match under its comparison rule", not "exact".
- **Dependencies.** Commitment 3.
- **Destination.** Body, after commitment 5 or folded into the illustration
  in commitment 9. Keep it brief.

## 9. Commonplace's quote checker as a single illustration

- **Commitment.** Commonplace mechanically checks `verbatim`-marked
  quotations against the Markdown source they link. That check illustrates
  commitment 8: it can falsify a false fidelity claim, but a pass shows only
  a normalized match against the linked text.
- **Treatment.** State it with a qualifier, as an explicitly scoped
  illustration. It is preferably one sentence. It is an illustration, not
  corroboration.
- **Basis.** C5 and S2, Decision ¶1. S2: `verbatim` is the only marker that
  can be mechanically falsified.
- **Scope and qualifiers.** Name it as Commonplace's choice so the
  collection's scoping rule holds. Do not list the normalization steps, the
  extraction heuristic, the `unresolved` rule or the code-fence exclusion.
  Do not explain the tracked/untracked storage design or its history. Link
  ADR 046 (and ADR 073 if cited) as `abstracted-from`, never as evidence that
  corroborates the claim. S1 is amended by ADRs 076 and 094 and records an
  earlier decision. Do not rely on S1's mechanism details.
- **Dependencies.** Commitment 8.
- **Destination.** One sentence attached to commitment 8. Source links go in
  the footer with `abstracted-from` labels. If either ADR is cited in the
  body, use it there as the origin.

## 10. The principle generalizes beyond Commonplace

- **Commitment.** The bound on a citation's fidelity by its capture holds
  for any citing practice, not only Commonplace's markers and validator.
- **Treatment.** State it as the note's universal hypothesis (I5). Do not
  present the ADRs as corroborating it.
- **Basis.** I5, the Scope section, and the collection contract ("Origin is
  not corroboration"; `abstracted-from`).
- **Scope and qualifiers.** Undeclared mode reads as universal. That is
  intended here. `## Scope` should say the claim was abstracted from one
  system's citation design and name the open gap: there is no finer test for
  when a bounded passage is enough.
- **Dependencies.** Commitments 3 to 8.
- **Destination.** Implicit in how the opening claim is phrased. Make it
  explicit in `## Scope` and through the footer `abstracted-from` labels.

## Commitments the note must not make

- Do not claim that any source states that a paraphrase preserves the idea
  while losing the words, or that quotation marks cannot recover words.
  These are the note's own argument (Gaps; I1).
- Do not attribute "narrow the citation" as a remedy to S1 or S2 (Gaps; I2).
- Do not cite S2's `paraphrase layer` and `second-hand` sentence as support.
  It cites this note, so using it would be circular (Conflicts).
- Do not equate a passed check with exact or byte identity (S2 internal
  tension).
- Do not claim that the check source is always available, or that location
  establishes availability (S2 Context ¶2; availability conflict). Do not
  explain the storage layers that cause this (excluded).
- Do not offer a finer decision rule than bounded versus broad, distributed
  or contextual (Gaps).
- Do not claim the checker is trustworthy or complete. S2 says its
  trustworthiness "needs separate support" and its extraction is incomplete.
- Do not use the prototype or corpus counts, legal or copyright reasoning, a
  survey of checking techniques, or instruction in how the validator works
  (commission exclusions).
- Do not define "fidelity" or "capture" as terms. No source defines them.
  Use them plainly.
- Reserved for the operator: the title and path stay as they are. Do not
  split the note or edit its dependents. Publication needs operator
  approval. This account does not decide any of these.

# A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

A writer reads a paper and keeps a note: the authors found that the method breaks down on long inputs. Weeks later, drafting an argument, the writer wants to write that the authors report the method "breaks down on long inputs". The quotation marks say these are the authors' words. The note cannot back that. It records what the writer took the passage to say, in the writer's words. The paper may have said that accuracy degrades on inputs longer than those seen in training, which is a narrower claim. A second writer who kept that sentence word for word can quote it.

A paraphrase can preserve an idea without preserving the author's words; rewording is what makes it a paraphrase. Rewording can also change the proposition, and the result is an interpretation, not source text. A direct quotation asserts that the quoted words are the source's own. If the capture, meaning what the writer retained, holds only a paraphrase, it contains no source words for the quotation marks to point to. Adding the marks claims fidelity the capture did not preserve, and no notation added later can recover words that were never kept. The same bound holds for any fidelity a citation claims, whether exact words, the idea, or the passage's place in its context. It matters because a reader who trusts the claimed fidelity may skip comparing the citation with the source and so miss the error.

The limit is on what a citation asserts about its evidence, not on what the writer may claim: the claim can still be made at the fidelity the capture supports, or as the writer's own.

## When the capture is enough

A bounded exact passage can be enough to judge some uses of a source, when the quoted words carry what the citing text relies on. Other uses depend on broad, distributed or contextual material, such as an overall argument, a pattern across sections or what surrounds the passage. A few retained passages cannot represent that material soundly; those uses need the full source.

The kind of check follows the kind of fidelity claimed. An exact-wording claim can be tested by matching words. A paraphrase makes no wording claim, so a wording check has nothing to match; checking it means judging whether the source supports it.

## What a passed wording check shows

A passed wording check shows that the quoted span matches the text actually compared, under the check's comparison rule. The pass is relative to that evidence. It does not certify that the compared text is the original author's words, that the span keeps its meaning in context, or that the quoted claim is true. When the text needed for the check is missing, the citation is unverified, not passed; counting absence as success would make the same citation pass or fail according to whatever copy happens to be at hand. Commonplace's quote checker illustrates the point: it can falsify a `verbatim`-marked quotation by matching it against the Markdown source the quotation links, and a pass means only a match under its normalization rule against that linked text ([ADR 046](../reference/adr/046-verbatim-quotes-are-validated-against-their-cited-source.md)).

## Narrow the citation or return to the source

A citation that claims no more than the capture preserved can stand on the capture: exact words that were kept, or a bounded use the retained passage carries. A citation that claims more has two honest exits. Narrow it to what the capture supports, by attributing a paraphrase instead of quoting or by making a narrower claim. Or return to the source and consult the evidence that supplies what is missing. Relying silently on material that is not at hand is not a third exit.

## Scope

- The claim was abstracted from one system's citation design (Commonplace's ADRs 046 and 073). Its transfer to other citing practices rests on the reasoning above, not on corroborating evidence.
- No test finer than bounded versus broad, distributed or contextual material decides when a retained passage is enough. Where that boundary falls for a given claim is open.
- The bound does not decide whether a failed wording check should block or only warn. Failing a quote on mismatch is a choice within the [trade-off between checking cost and reliance risk](./checking-retained-results-trades-cost-against-reliance-risk.md).

# Review a rewrite candidate

Goal: the candidate reaches the operator's publication stop only when an
independent reviewer finds that this exact text makes the commissioned
contribution on the evidence, within the contracts. The findings that do not
block reach the operator before publication and can be triaged after it.

Consumption: the rewrite workflow (`commonplace-review run rewrite`) runs a
review operation with this file as its criterion, in the `review` step and,
after one repair, in the `review-repair` step. A fresh headless worker
receives this file as the criterion, the candidate as the note's text, and the
other inputs below as operational inputs. The prompt names the inputs, the
review-result contract and the output file. Nothing else is inherited.

## Inputs

- The note's text input: the candidate, the exact text to judge. It is not
  the note's current file.
- `candidate-report`: the author's report of what it kept, replaced and
  omitted from the existing note.
- `commission`: the operator's current direction for this rewrite and the
  sources with their roles. When the note has no write brief, it also states
  the intended contribution and reader update, what to keep and exclude, and
  the decisions reserved for the operator. When the note has a brief, it
  holds only what this rewrite adds to the brief, and it names any brief item
  the operator amended for this rewrite.
- `brief`, when present: the note's write brief. It is binding retained
  intent. Its Intent, Must keep, Must exclude and Reserved decisions hold
  together with the commission's additions. A commission that only adds to
  the brief does not contradict it.
- `reconstruction`: the source-faithful basis.
- `claim-account`: how the note was to treat each commitment of the
  reconstruction.
- `start`: the note's text when the run started.
- `type-contract` and `collection-contract`, when present: the contracts the
  note must meet.
- `kb-role`, when present: the `## Role` section of the note's role report.
  It says which of the note's terms and claims other notes rely on.
- `earlier-decisions`, when present: the operator's decisions in earlier
  revise and rewrite runs on this note, with the operator's reasons.
- `finding-decisions`, when present: the findings of earlier reviews of this
  note against this instruction that the operator rejected, with the rule
  for raising one again.

## What you must not do

- Do not edit the candidate or any file. Write nothing except the output
  file.
- Do not choose the repair. Say what must change; the author changes it.
- Do not read the note's file in the checkout, earlier runs or earlier
  reviews. Judge the inputs.

## Procedure

Check, in this order:

1. The delta from `start` to the candidate against the claim account and
   the report: every material commitment of the existing note is kept,
   replaced or omitted with a reason, and no commitment appears that the
   claim account does not give.
2. The commission and the brief: the intended contribution, what must be
   kept and excluded, and no reserved decision taken.
3. The note's dependents and the operator's earlier decisions. Report as a
   finding a term or claim `kb-role` lists as relied on that the candidate
   renames, redefines or drops, unless the commission's current direction
   asks for it and the report says so. Report as a finding a candidate that
   reintroduces a change the operator rejected in `earlier-decisions`, or
   drops a wording the operator approved there, unless the commission's
   current direction says otherwise. Content `kb-role` lists as unused is
   not for that reason a finding.
4. The contracts: the type and the collection.
5. Evidence: each claim has the support or the inference the reconstruction
   gives, with its scope and qualifiers.
6. Specificity, relevance and prose.

A finding blocks when the candidate cannot be published without the change.
A finding about missing evidence says that the sources lack it; the session
agent then grounds or adds a source and starts again.

## Output

Write a review result as the supplied review-result contract defines it:

1. Each finding has `scope`, `quotes`, `reason` and `level`.
   - `scope: passage` with `quotes` holding the passage of the candidate the
     finding anchors to, verbatim and occurring once. Use `scope: document`
     with empty `quotes` for an absence, such as a dropped commitment.
   - `reason` states `Basis:`, the input and passage that show the problem,
     and then `Required change:`, the change the candidate needs.
   - `level: fail` for a finding that blocks; `level: warn` for one that
     asks for a change but does not block; `level: info` for a remark that
     asks for no change.
2. `outcome: fail` when any finding has level `fail`: the candidate is
   blocked. Otherwise `outcome: warn` when a finding has level `warn`, and
   `outcome: pass` when no finding asks for a change. Code refuses an
   outcome that does not match the levels, and a `warn` or `fail` finding
   whose reason lacks `Basis:` or `Required change:`.
3. A `# Review` body that explains the judgment without repeating each
   finding.

Code binds the result to the candidate through its target hash. A `warn`
result reaches the publication stop; the operator hears of its findings
before deciding. When the operator publishes this exact candidate, the result
becomes the note's current result, and a triage presents its `warn` findings.

# Review result

A review result records one assessment of captured target text against a criterion. Completion means the output passed deterministic checks, not that its judgment is correct. A report outcome is not a favorable verdict. Use this type for individual gate, compression-check, type-conformance and collection-conformance verdicts, and for critique, composition-friction, premise-decomposition and compression-synthesis reports and role reports. Do not use it for combined improvement packets or connection discovery.

## Content

Findings state what the assessed text establishes or fails to establish. Each passage finding quotes enough verbatim text to identify one contiguous span uniquely. A quote is matched after whitespace and typographic quote marks are normalized, so a line wrap in the target does not break it. A quote therefore identifies a passage and is not a byte-exact copy of it. A consumer that needs the exact span locates the quote in the captured target, which holds the exact bytes. A document-wide or absence finding explains the condition without inventing a quotation. Finding levels belong to verdict criteria; critique reports instead state whether the strongest attack lands and how the note engages it. An empty findings list is an honest completed result when no finding remains.

The body explains the assessment without repeating every structured finding. A critique preserves its central commitment, critique mode, strongest case, the note's response and constructive findings, including why an attack does not survive. Low-confidence no-surviving-attack findings leave the need for a domain check visible.

Each report method has its own shape, which the schema checks by the result's `criterion`:

| Method | Findings | Required body |
|---|---|---|
| Critique | constructive findings | `attack-outcome` in frontmatter; `## Strongest case against it`, `## How the note engages it`, `## Constructive findings` |
| Composition friction | the surfaced joints, thinnest first; each reason begins `UNSUPPORTED`, `THIN` or `HOLDS` | a `**Filter:** SURVIVES` or `DISSOLVES` line; `## Filter`, `## Thinnest joints`, `## For the human` |
| Premise decomposition | one per premise; each reason begins `HOLDS`, `DOUBTFUL` or `DEFEATED`, and a non-`HOLDS` reason names `LOCAL` or `GLOBAL` and `instance`, `prevalence` or `priced-exception` | a `**Register:**` line; `## Premises and counterexamples`, `## For the human` |
| Compression synthesis | zero to three opportunities | `## Opportunities` |
| Role report | one per dependent need, duplication or untaken recommendation; each reason begins `SUPPLIED`, `PARTLY SUPPLIED`, `NOT SUPPLIED`, `DUPLICATED` or `UNTAKEN` | `## Role`, `## Dependents`, `## Duplication`, `## Untaken recommendations`, `## Reach` |

Only critique supplies `attack-outcome`. Friction's filter line and the premise statuses route attention; they are not overall verdicts. A report criterion is named by its library instruction's identity, so moving one of these instructions requires a schema edit.

## Field ownership

The worker fragment supplies only `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, optional `attack-outcome`, and the body. Findings precede the outcome so the serialized verdict follows its rationale. The fragment is not a complete saved artifact. The controller completes and validates it; workers never assert hashes, execution identities or timestamps.

| Fields | Owner and meaning |
|---|---|
| `type`, `findings`, `outcome`, `attack-outcome` | Worker assessment; findings contain `scope`, `quotes`, `reason`, and `level` for verdicts |
| `description`, `format`, `contract` | Controller's result-format identity and expected verdict/report contract |
| `note`, `criterion` | Original target and criterion identities |
| `note-sha256`, `criterion-sha256` | Freshness hashes; the note hash may cover normalized watched parts, not exact bytes |
| `target-sha256`, `target-capture` | Exact assessed UTF-8 bytes and their retained repository-relative location |
| `observation`, `contract-sha256` | Execution observation and captured output-contract identity |
| `profile`, `model`, `run`, `launch`, `completed-at` | Requested execution configuration and observed execution provenance |
| `raw-output`, `raw-output-sha256` | Retained original worker fragment, distinct from this completed artifact |

## Template

Worker fragment for a verdict criterion; code supplies the remaining fields:

```markdown
---
type: types/review-result.md
findings:
  - scope: document
    quotes: []
    reason: "The claim omits the condition needed for its stated conclusion."
    level: warn
outcome: warn
---

# Review

## Summary

The conclusion needs its missing condition.
```

A critique fragment uses `outcome: report`, supplies `attack-outcome`, and omits finding levels. Its body retains the critique instruction's sections. Other report fragments use `outcome: report`, omit `attack-outcome` and finding levels, and follow their instruction's Output section. Neither fragment uses a terminal `## Result:` line. Operational production and publication belong to the review command, not to this type.

# Writing conventions for kb/reports/ (report collection)

## Purpose and scope

This collection contains analytical outputs, evaluation records, and local
operational evidence that are consumed as reports rather than as library
claims or system definitions. Placement here is justified by the output's
retention policy and consumer, not by its filename or by the fact that a tool
generated it.

A report belongs here only when a named operation consumes the report itself.
Transferable claims belong in `kb/theory/`; descriptions of the shipped system
and its decisions belong in `kb/reference/`; executable procedures belong in
`kb/instructions/`; and reasoning whose value is consumed by unfinished work
belongs in `kb/work/`.

## Policy areas

Every report artifact lives in exactly one first-level policy area:

| Area | Retention policy | Typical contents |
|---|---|---|
| `state/` | Ignored, one directory per producing workflow. Not disposable merely because it was generated: the owning workflow decides when an output may be removed, and the [state README](./state/README.md) states per workflow what deletion loses. | Review results, packets and runs; fix dispositions; ingest working directories; connect, critique, friction, premise-decomposition and promotion-candidate reports. |
| `retained/` | Durable report records kept with the project. Payloads are tracked. | Evaluation corpora, experiment reports, measurements, and exact records cited by later work. |
| `types/` | Collection-local structural contracts, not report payloads. | Optional project-authored report contracts; command-produced generic report types are global. |

The published site includes `retained/` and leaves out `state/`. Inside `retained/`, a subtree carrying a
`.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker is left out of the site as well as
validation; mark exact captures and trial bundles so, keeping the report that
interprets them published.

Do not put report payloads directly at the collection root. Moving an artifact
between policy areas is a change in its retention contract, not a filing-only
rename.

## Quality goal

Make the report sufficient for the operation that consumes it without making
it impersonate a durable knowledge claim. State the subject, inputs or source
state, method, result, and material limits to the degree needed to interpret
or reproduce the output. Record the model and prompt or instruction identity
when an LLM judgment is part of the evidence and the producing workflow does
not already retain them.

`state/` must satisfy the owning workflow's authority, integrity, and cleanup
rules. `retained/` must remain
understandable from a clean checkout without relying on ignored files.

## Titles, descriptions, and exact records

- Use a title that names the analysis, experiment, or result. A title such as
  "Report" does not distinguish the artifact.
- When frontmatter is present, write a retrieval-oriented `description` that
  identifies the subject and why the exact output is retained.
- Frontmatter-free Markdown is permitted for deliberate unstructured output.
- Preserve an exact capture when fidelity is the report's purpose. If a copied
  artifact carries another collection's local type only as captured data, put
  a `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at the capture-set root rather than
  presenting that copy as a live typed artifact of this collection.

## Maintenance semantics

- A state producer owns cleanup and states, in the state README, what deleting
  its output loses: nothing unique (rebuild from retained inputs), one paid
  judgment (rerun when needed) or current coverage, an unresolved disposition
  or decision evidence (preserve). Generated state may contain non-reproducible
  judgments or the only current disposition, so Git ignore status never
  licenses deletion.
- A retained report is changed according to its declared role. Correct a
  living report in place; preserve a dated or frozen observation as an exact
  record and create a new observation when the measured state changes.
- Local evidence notes are the one interpreted form `retained/` keeps as
  durable artifacts: a `types/note.md` artifact whose bounded inference
  concerns only Commonplace's own choices or their measured effects, beside
  the raw records it interprets. Its formal edges use this collection's labels
  below. An inference that keeps a free variable belongs in
  `kb/theory/evidence/`.
- If a report develops a transferable claim, binding rule, system premise, or
  unfinished-work lifecycle, extract that content to its proper collection.
  Do not broaden `retained/` into a second notes, reference, instructions, or
  workshop collection.

## Outbound links

Reports may inspect any project surface. Use relative Markdown links for live
navigation and state in prose why the target matters. Inline links may carry
ordinary evidential or procedural context. Footer-shaped formal edges use this
small authorized set:

| label | destinations | reader need |
|---|---|---|
| `derived-from` | sources, external | inspect the source material from which the report was produced |
| `is-evidence-for` | theory, reference, reports | inspect the durable claim, decision, or report record on which this output bears |
| `compares-with` | theory, reference, sources, reports | compare two artifacts on a named shared axis |
| `see-also` | any durable collection, external | inspect useful adjacent context when no stronger relation applies |

The destination collection separately decides whether it may author a
reciprocal edge. A formal edge into this collection targets `retained/`;
`state/` may be mentioned inline only as local operational context.

Tracked library artifacts must not depend on an ignored `state/` file being
present. Summarize the needed evidence in the tracked artifact or
promote the exact report to `retained/` first. Tracked artifacts may cite a
`retained/` report when the exact record is useful to their reader.

## Validation markers

The tracked `.commonplace-validation-ignore` marker at `state/` excludes its
data-bearing subtree from collection-scoped validation. The marker does not
hide files from ordinary discovery, and explicit validation of
one typed report still applies its type contract.

A file under `state/` may declare any valid type spec, including another
collection's local type. Workflows stage candidates there for other
collections, and a candidate must validate against its destination's contract.
The type spec itself stays in the owning collection's `types/` directory.
`retained/` does not share this exception.

## What does not belong here

- A generated explanation or synthesis whose claim should survive the run →
  `kb/theory/` or `kb/reference/` according to its consumer.
- A procedure named "report" because it produces one → `kb/instructions/`.
- Drafts, deliberation, and run traces consumed by an unfinished investigation
  → `kb/work/`.
- External source captures and their durable analyses → `kb/sources/`.
- Build outputs with no report consumer → their build cache, not `kb/reports/`.
